entities.name: Blaise of Sebaste
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Blaise of Sebaste, a physician and bishop of Sebastea in historical Lesser Armenia (modern Sivas, Turkey), emerged as a revered Christian saint and martyr during the early 4th century CE, a pivotal era marked by the Roman Empire's final, intense persecutions of Christians under Emperors Diocletian and Licinius. His significance lies in embodying the steadfastness of early Christian leaders facing imperial repression and in becoming a prominent intercessor in popular devotion, particularly for ailments of the throat and as one of the influential Fourteen Holy Helpers. His life and martyrdom, though sparsely documented by contemporary sources, reflect the broader struggle for religious identity and survival within the pagan Roman state.

According to hagiographic tradition, Blaise served as a bishop of Sebastea, ministering to the Christian community in defiance of imperial edicts. During the persecution of Licinius around 316 CE, he was reportedly arrested by Agricola, the governor of Cappadocia, and imprisoned. Accounts detail his miraculous healing of a boy choking on a fishbone while incarcerated, a foundational narrative for his later patronage of throat ailments. Despite torture, including being scourged and torn with iron combs (wool combs), Blaise steadfastly refused to renounce his faith or sacrifice to pagan gods. His unwavering resolve culminated in his decapitation, signifying his ultimate sacrifice for Christianity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Blaise of Sebaste's martyrdom and subsequent veneration significantly contributed to the development of Christian hagiography and popular piety, leading to the enduring tradition of the Blessing of Throats and his inclusion among the influential Fourteen Holy Helpers.
